body:
INFORMED RESPONSE TO THE OWNER LINK — this paper is the bar to beat, not a paper to wave away.

I read the methods and results, not only the abstract. Panela et al. test three roughly 1,500-word excerpts from one memoir. The main sample is 20 younger adults; a separate 11-person sample rates GPT-selected boundary and non-boundary locations. They run GPT-4 and LLaMA 20 times at three temperatures to study segmentation agreement. For recall scoring, however, both each source narrative and each recall transcript receive normative GPT-4 temperature-0 boundaries. Each source-event row is scored by its maximum embedding correlation with any recall segment, and those maxima are averaged.

That is a useful, legible baseline. It is not the problem storymodel4s claims to solve.

The exact gap is:

1. ONE SELECTED CUT. Model variability is measured, but admissible cuts are not propagated into recall results. The paper itself says averaging model instances may mitigate nondeterminism; it does not ask whether different lawful cuts change the scientific conclusion.

2. BEST-MATCH GIST, NOT ALIGNMENT. Row-wise maxima let one recall segment serve as the best match for several source events. There is no transport budget, omission cost, external or intrusion destination, hierarchy, or explicit reordering trajectory.

3. ONE SCORE HIDES THE ERROR TYPE. Their validation target is human gist rating. The score cannot say whether the actor, role, action, polarity, context, modality, or temporal placement was preserved. A fluent role reversal can remain semantically close.

4. NO CONSTRUCTION AUTHORITY. GPT choice, prompt, temperature, and repeated outputs matter to the analysis, but the resulting recall number does not carry a resolver-minted authority that prevents baseline, adjudicated, and provider-resolved constructions from being pooled.

5. LIMITED GENERALIZATION CLAIM. Three passages from one English memoir and 20 recall participants are a proof of feasibility, not a cross-story, cross-population, or clinical validation. The reported standardized relations with human ratings are beta 0.36 to 0.52; the corrected consistencies are 0.52 to 0.64. There is room to improve, but beating a coefficient on the same small sample would not establish our thesis.

Here is the experiment that could make "much better" true:

A. Reproduce their open pipeline and data exactly as a named baseline: normative GPT cut plus row-maximum embedding score.
B. Freeze independent multi-rater, multi-grain boundary gold and held-out stories before tuning.
C. Compare point-cut baseline, point-cut GraphHsmm, and alternative-preserving GraphHsmm under the same providers and embedding budget.
D. Score boundary calibration and coverage; event-level gist; omission and intrusion detection; chronology; role/polarity/context errors; and held-out behavioral or clinical criteria.
E. Run the uncertainty ablation that their paper does not: one chosen cut versus retained alternatives or complete-artifact sensitivity. The stronger method wins only if it improves calibration, detects conclusion changes, or makes genuinely robust conclusions more stable.
F. Repeat across story genres, populations, and at least one provider shift. Bind every result to source spans, construction policy, provider/configuration receipts, and support.

If alternative-preserving alignment does not beat the simple row-max pipeline on those outcomes, then our extra structure is ceremony. If it does, the contribution is precise: not a superior cutter, but an auditable recall estimand whose conclusions remain honest when segmentation and interpretation are uncertain.

Primary source: https://www.nature.com/articles/s44271-025-00359-7

No bead, implementation authority, type name, path, or SOTA claim is asserted here.
